history.hypothesis: JobRegistry is a global singleton whose state leaks between test methods: when a sibling test (e.g. assertRemoveLocalInstancePath) registers 'test_job' and never shuts the JobRegistry entry down, the InstanceShutdownStatusJobListener in assertIsShutdownAlready sees an active, non-shutdown local instance and invokes schedulerFacade.shutdownInstance(), violating the times(0) assertion.

diagnosis.root_cause: JobRegistry is a process-wide singleton whose per-job registration state is shared across tests. The polluter test assertRemoveLocalInstancePath registers the job via JobRegistry.getInstance().registerJob(...) but never calls JobRegistry.getInstance().shutdown("test_job"), so the job remains registered. When assertIsShutdownAlready then runs, the InstanceShutdownStatusJobListener finds the job already registered and invokes schedulerFacade.shutdownInstance(), violating the times(0) verification.

evidence.why: This test registers the job in the global JobRegistry singleton but never unregisters/shuts it down, leaving shared state that leaks into subsequent tests in the same JVM.

This test assumes the job is NOT registered, so the listener should no-op. Because the previous test leaked a registered job into the singleton, the listener instead calls schedulerFacade.shutdownInstance(), producing the NeverWantedButInvoked failure at ShutdownListenerManagerTest.java:60.

The listener consults the global JobRegistry for the job's registered instance; the polluter's leaked registration makes these guards pass and triggers shutdownInstance(), which the failing stack trace attributes to ShutdownListenerManager.java:61.

history.hypothesis: EnumTester.iterations is a static field that is never reset, so any re-execution of the test in the same JVM (or a prior run of the same class) leaves a stale accumulated value, making assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), iterations) fail.

diagnosis.root_cause: EnumTester.iterations is a static field that is never reset, and each run of the JUnitQuickcheck property executes 100 trials incrementing it. When the test is re-executed in the same JVM (e.g. runs=2), the counter accumulates 100+100=200, so the assertion comparing against defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100) fails on the second execution.

evidence.why: The counter is static and monotonically incremented with no reset, so it carries state across repeated executions in the same JVM.
This asserts the accumulated static counter equals exactly the per-run trial count (100), which is only true on the first execution; the second run yields 200 as observed.

history.hypothesis: PrimitiveDoubles (and several sibling tests) mutate static fields `iterations`/`values` without resetting them, so any re-execution of the test class in the same JVM accumulates state and the `assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), PrimitiveDoubles.iterations)` assertion fails.

diagnosis.root_cause: The nested PrimitiveDoubles property class keeps its run count in a static mutable field (PrimitiveDoubles.iterations) that is never reset between executions of the enclosing test method. When the test method is invoked a second time in the same JVM it adds another 100 trials on top of the leftover 100, so the assertion expects defaultPropertyTrialCount() (100) but observes 200. This makes the test non-idempotent: it only passes the first time it runs in a JVM.

evidence.why: iterations is a static field accumulated inside the property; because primitiveDoubles never zeroes it (unlike primitiveBooleans/primitiveBytes which end with `X.iterations = 0;`), a repeated invocation in the same JVM double-counts to 200.
This is the exact failing assertion in the stack trace (expected:<100> but was:<200>); the value is 200 because the static counter retained the previous run's 100 trials.
Contrast: sibling tests explicitly reset their static counters after asserting, showing that shared static state is the intended but forgotten reset for primitiveDoubles.

diagnosis.root_cause: The nested property class PrimitiveBytes keeps its run counter in a static field `iterations` that is never reset between executions. Each call to `testResult(PrimitiveBytes.class)` adds 100 trials to the same static counter, so when the test method is executed a second time in the same JVM the assertion `assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), PrimitiveBytes.iterations)` sees 200 instead of the expected 100 and fails.

evidence.why: The test re-executes a nested JUnitQuickcheck property run (via testResult) whose state is held in static fields, so re-running the same method in one JVM does not start from a clean state.
This is the exact line in the failure stack; it asserts the counter equals 100 but observes 200 because the accumulator was not reset between runs.
The static `iterations` counter and static `values` list are mutated on every trial and are never cleared, so a second execution in the same JVM accumulates (100 -> 200) and produces the mismatch.

The first execution inserts the unique row with task id 'fake_failover_task_id', so on the second execution the precondition assertion at line 68 (size is 0) sees the leftover row and fails non-deterministically depending on how many times the test has already run in the JVM.

evidence.snippet: BasicDataSource dataSource = new BasicDataSource(); ... dataSource.setUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:job_event_storage"); ... storage = new RDBJobEventStorage(dataSource);
evidence.why: The named in-memory database 'job_event_storage' is a JVM-wide singleton shared across all test instances/runs and is never dropped; pooled connections keep it alive so state written by one execution is visible to the next.

The stack trace points to line 68 (the failure). On a repeated execution in the same JVM the row for 'fake_failover_task_id' from the prior run is still present, so the initial size-is-0 assertion fails even though no new insert has happened yet.

history.hypothesis: PrimitiveChars.iterations (a static field) is incremented by the JUnitQuickcheck run but is never reset after the assertion (unlike PrimitiveBooleans/PrimitiveBytes which do reset), so re-executing the test method in the same JVM accumulates the count and the second run's assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), PrimitiveChars.iterations) fails.

diagnosis.root_cause: The static field PrimitiveChars.iterations is incremented by the inner @Property every time testResult(PrimitiveChars.class) executes, but unlike primitiveBooleans/primitiveBytes this test never resets the counter back to 0. When the test class is executed a second time in the same JVM (runs=2), the counter starts at 100 and ends at 200, so assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), PrimitiveChars.iterations) expects 100 but sees 200.

evidence.why: This method reads PrimitiveChars.iterations (line 165, the failing assertion) and does not reset it to 0, unlike primitiveBooleans (PrimitiveBooleans.iterations = 0) and primitiveBytes (PrimitiveBytes.iterations = 0) which follow the same pattern but do reset. The lack of reset is exactly what makes a second in-JVM execution accumulate to 200.
The static counter is only ever incremented (`++iterations`) and never reset, so its value persists across repeated runs in the same JVM, causing the 100 -> 200 accumulation observed in the failure.

evidence.why: A fixed-name in-memory H2 database is used each run and the dataSource is never closed; because connections stay open the DB is not dropped between executions, so rows written by the first run survive into the second run.

history.hypothesis: The test class keeps mutable static state (per-property `values`/`iterations` lists/counters) that is only partially reset, so the assertion on `values.subList(0,2)` and `assertEquals(defaultPropertyTrialCount(), iterations)` can fail when the class/property is executed more than once in the same JVM (non-idempotent, order-dependent state accumulation).

diagnosis.root_cause: The test re-runs the PrimitiveFloats property class in the same JVM, whose static `iterations` counter is never reset to 0 (unlike primitiveBooleans/primitiveBytes which do `iterations = 0`). After the first execution the counter already holds 100, and the second execution increments it another 100 trials to 200, so the assertion `defaultPropertyTrialCount()` (100) against the accumulated 200 fails. The failure is thus a non-idempotent second-run outcome driven by un-reset static test-fixture state.

evidence.why: Stack trace shows the AssertionError at this line expecting 100 but observing 200, i.e. the static counter holds the sum of two runs.

Contrast: the boolean variant explicitly resets its static counter after asserting, preventing cross-run accumulation. primitiveFloats lacks this reset, so a second in-JVM execution doubles the count.

evidence.snippet: public static class PrimitiveFloats { static int iterations; ... @Property(mode = EXHAUSTIVE) public void shouldHold(@Also(...) @From(AFloat.class) float f) { values.add(f); ++iterations; } }
evidence.why: The static `iterations` field is mutated by each property trial and never reset (either at end of test method or in @Before), so state persists across repeated executions of the test in the same JVM.

diagnosis.root_cause: The static field `iterations` inside the nested `BoxOfFoo` class is never reset between test executions. When the test method `boxOfFoo` runs a second time in the same JVM, the counter still holds 100 from the first execution, so the 100 property trials bring it to 200, and the assertion expecting `defaultPropertyTrialCount()` (100) fails with 200.

evidence.why: A static counter persists across test runs in the same JVM, accumulating trial counts from previous executions instead of starting at 0.
Each property trial increments the shared static counter, so a second run adds another 100 to the already-nonzero value.
This assertion, which failed in the reproduction (expected 100 but was 200), checks the accumulated counter and fails when it contains trials from a prior execution.

When the same test method (and thus the same JVM/static state) is run more than once, the second run starts with the 100 elements left over from the first run, so values.size() becomes 200 and the assertion `defaultPropertyTrialCount() == values.size()` fails with expected:<100> but was:<200>.

evidence.snippet: static final List<TestEnum> values = new ArrayList<>();

This assertion assumes the list contains exactly one run's worth of trials; on the second execution it observes 2x and fails (expected 100 but was 200).

history.hypothesis: Gson serializes CastleContext fields by reflecting over Class.getDeclaredFields(), whose iteration order is not guaranteed by the JVM, so under non-deterministic class-member/reflection ordering the 'library' and 'active' fields may emit in a different order and break the exact-string equality against SDKVersion.getLibraryString().

diagnosis.root_cause: The test asserts that the serialized CastleContext JSON string is exactly equal to the string produced by SDKVersion.getLibraryString(), which builds the "library" object in a fixed key order (name, version, platform, platform_version). The actual JSON is produced by Gson serializing the underlying library representation, whose entries are held in a hash-based structure, so the key order within the "library" object is nondeterministic. When the iteration/field order differs from the hard-coded order in getLibraryString(), isEqualTo fails even though the JSON content is semantically identical.

evidence.why: The assertion is an exact String comparison of Gson-serialized output against SDKVersion.getLibraryString(). Because the values are equal but the key order inside "library" differs, only a byte-for-byte string comparison would fail — exactly the observed ComparisonFailure where the pieces inside library:{...} are permuted (e.g. platform_version before name etc.).

evidence.snippet: SDKVersion.getLibraryString() // builds "library":{"name":...,"version":...,"platform":...,"platform_version":...} in a hard-coded order
evidence.why: The expected side always emits name, version, platform, platform_version in that fixed order (as seen in every failure's 'expected' half), while the actual Gson output of the library object arrives in varying orders across the reproduced rounds, confirming the nondeterminism lives in how the library map/object is serialized, not in the expected builder.

The library object is what Gson serializes; because its entries are stored/iterated in a hash-based (unordered) fashion, the emitted JSON member order varies per execution, causing the exact-string equality assertion to fail intermittently.

history.hypothesis: The expected string hard-codes the reflection field order (boolArray, charArray, intArray, doubleArray, longArray, stringArray) of WithArrays, but ReflectionToStringBuilder relies on Class.getDeclaredFields()/getFields() whose ordering is not guaranteed by the JVM spec, so a nondeterminism-injecting run (NonDex) can reorder the fields and break the assertion.
